title: trapdoor
goal: trapdoor is a synthetic ticketing service that exists to be MAPPED WRONG. Every directory in it plants a defect class that four real coyomap builds produced, so a regression suite can assert what the map tooling says about a real tree rather than about a toy in-memory object. Support agents move tickets through a declared lifecycle, reporters comment on them, and a background worker rolls resolved tickets up; that product story is only realistic enough to hang the traps on.

roles.wants: to add context to a ticket they raised and see what happened to it

roles.name: Support agent
roles.wants: to work a tenant's queue: find tickets, read them, and move them along the lifecycle

use_cases.name: Browse a tenant's tickets
use_cases.trigger: An agent asks for a tenant's queue, optionally filtered by state
use_cases.outcome: they get the list of tickets they are allowed to see, each with its state and comment count.

use_cases.name: Read one ticket
use_cases.trigger: Someone opens a ticket by id
use_cases.outcome: they see its title, state, assignee and its comment thread, or a 404 when the ticket belongs to another tenant.

use_cases.name: Move a ticket along its lifecycle
use_cases.trigger: An agent posts a target state
use_cases.outcome: the transition is checked against the declared table, the ticket is stored in its new state, re-indexed, and a state-change event is published.

use_cases.name: Comment on a ticket
use_cases.trigger: A reporter posts text on a ticket they may write
use_cases.outcome: the comment is appended to the ticket document and the thread comes back one longer.

use_cases.name: Take an advisory lock
use_cases.trigger: An operator claims a named lock before a bulk job
use_cases.outcome: the lock row records the holder, so a second claim can see who holds it.

happy_path.why: needs a ticket id from the queue listed in HP1
the ticket opened in HP2 is the one being commented on
the comment thread from HP3 is what the agent read before deciding

subsystems.name: Ticket workflow
subsystems.purpose: Everything that answers a ticket request end to end: the HTTP handlers, the application service that orchestrates them, and the repository that is the system of record. This is where traps O1 and O2 live: the handlers look like they own the datastore and do not.

subsystems.name: Eventing
subsystems.purpose: The asynchronous half: the publisher that names three channels, the one consumer that drains a channel, and the plugin family that reacts. Traps M1-M4 are all here.

subsystems.name: Notification plugins
subsystems.purpose: Eight identically-shaped plugin directories, each listening on one channel and forwarding a shaped payload to the analytics sink. A homogeneous family: it reads as a list, not as eight decisions.

subsystems.name: Platform runtime
subsystems.purpose: The cross-cutting machinery every request and every worker pass runs through: authorisation, the lifecycle table, escalation policy, the worker template and its one concrete worker, the client factory, and the two process entry points.

subsystems.name: Shared validation
subsystems.purpose: A flat toolkit of value validators. Past both leaf caps with no subdirectory to recurse into, so it is split into two cohesive components rather than folded into one box (trap G2).

subsystems.name: Web UI
subsystems.purpose: The browser half: a file-per-component presentational tree plus its hyperscript runtime. The FILE cap binds here, so the code-derived expectation E lands far above the honest altitude (trap G1).

components.name: Ticket read handlers
components.purpose: The read side of the HTTP surface: fetch one ticket, list a tenant's queue, list a thread. Every handler authorises, then forwards to the ticket service and renders the result. It owns no collection and issues no store call of its own.

components.name: Ticket write handlers
components.purpose: The mutating HTTP surface: transition a ticket, append a comment, claim a lock. It calls .save() through the service, which is exactly why it reads like the system of record without being one.

components.name: Ticket service
components.purpose: Application logic for the ticket lifecycle: tenant-scoped fetch, listing, transition-and-announce, comment append, and lock acquisition. The component that really holds the repository and the publisher.

components.name: Ticket repository
components.purpose: The system of record for tickets, comments and attachments. It issues every document-store call in the fixture: the ticket upsert, the secondary search-index write, and the advisory lock rows.

components.name: Authorisation gate
components.purpose: Decides whether a principal may read or write a tenant's tickets. The write check composes scope, tenant and lifecycle state into one predicate and raises far below its own header.

components.name: Lifecycle table
components.purpose: The declared ticket states and the transition table between them, plus the guard that refuses an illegal move. The one lifecycle in this tree that a states machine may cite.

components.name: Escalation policy
components.purpose: Counts breaches against a retry budget and decides whether to page. Its docstring describes a five-phase lifecycle that no code implements.

components.name: Event publisher
components.purpose: Publishes three named channels through an injected transport. Because the transport is a seam, this component names no broker library anywhere in its own code.

components.name: Comment consumer
components.purpose: The only consumer in the tree: a continuous loop that drains the comment channel and fans each message out to registered handlers.

components.name: Worker template
components.purpose: The abstract template method every background worker follows: prepare, do the subclass work, record. It is never deployed on its own.

components.name: Report worker
components.purpose: The one concrete worker: sweeps each tenant's tickets on a cron schedule and produces a resolved-ticket rollup.

components.name: Client factory
components.purpose: Reads configuration and hands back configured analytics and error-sink handles. Constructing a client opens no socket and sends nothing.

components.name: Retry policy
components.purpose: Exponential backoff with a ceiling, plus the retry header it produces. Imports two types it never uses.

components.name: HTTP process entry
components.purpose: The api unit's process entry point: a minimal route table whose six registrations are the whole external HTTP surface.

components.name: Worker process entry
components.purpose: The worker unit's process entry point: builds the consumer, reads the cron schedule and supervises worker passes. Self-activated only.

components.name: Slack plugin
components.purpose: Reacts to the Slack notification channel and forwards a shaped payload to the analytics sink.

components.name: Teams plugin
components.purpose: Reacts to the Microsoft Teams notification channel and forwards a shaped payload to the analytics sink.

components.name: Audit plugin
components.purpose: Reacts to the ticket state-change channel, under the hyphenated spelling of the same channel name the publisher declares with dots.

components.name: Email digest plugin
components.purpose: Reacts to the email notification channel and forwards a shaped payload to the analytics sink.

components.name: Outbound webhook plugin
components.purpose: Reacts to the webhook notification channel and forwards a shaped payload to the analytics sink.

components.name: Pager rota plugin
components.purpose: Reacts to the pager notification channel and forwards a shaped payload to the analytics sink.

components.name: Metrics rollup plugin
components.purpose: Reacts to the metrics notification channel and forwards a shaped payload to the analytics sink.

components.name: Cold archive plugin
components.purpose: Reacts to the archive notification channel and forwards a shaped payload to the analytics sink.

components.name: Scalar validators
components.purpose: Validation and normalisation for quantitative value types: currency amounts, durations, percentages and version strings. One of the two cohesive groups the oversized flat folder splits into.

components.name: Text validators
components.purpose: Validation and normalisation for textual value types: email addresses, host names, identifiers, markdown, phone numbers, postcodes, timezones and urls. The second group the flat folder splits into.

components.name: Generated wire types
components.purpose: Machine-emitted message classes carrying an @generated banner. Heavy by weight, one box by judgement: the whole directory is regenerated from a schema and holds no decision a reader needs.

components.name: Ticket UI components
components.purpose: Fourteen tiny presentational components — one file each — rendering the ticket list, a ticket row, the comment thread and the surrounding chrome.

components.name: Web runtime
components.purpose: The minimal hyperscript helper every UI component builds its tree with.

deps.name: MongoDB
deps.used_for: Stores the ticket documents, their embedded comment threads, and the advisory lock rows. The system of record for everything the product remembers.

deps.name: Redis
deps.used_for: Carries the three named channels the publisher writes and the one the consumer drains.

deps.name: OpenSearch
deps.used_for: Holds a denormalised copy of each ticket's title, body and tenant so the queue can be searched. Shares its name with the compose service that runs it.

deps.name: Analytics SaaS
deps.used_for: Receives one event per plugin reaction. The client is built centrally and used by the eight plugins.

deps.name: Error reporting SaaS
deps.used_for: Receives unhandled exceptions. Its client is constructed by the factory and, in this fixture, wired to nothing else.

entities.name: Ticket
entities.meaning: A unit of work raised by a reporter and worked by an assignee, carrying its position in the declared lifecycle.

entities.name: Comment
entities.meaning: A note appended to a ticket. Embedded in its ticket document rather than stored as its own row.

entities.name: Attachment
entities.meaning: A file hung off a comment. Only the pointer is stored here; the bytes live in object storage.

store.notes: rides the comment that rides the ticket

entities.name: AuditEntry
entities.meaning: An immutable record of one ticket state change. TRAP P1: nothing in this fixture persists it, so it lands in the no-owning-component advisory, which offers no recordable escape.

store.notes: appended through the generic plugin bus, so no component carries a write edge to it

entities.name: LockDoc
entities.meaning: An advisory lock row recording who holds a named lock and until when.

store.notes: infra-only; named by no use case narrative

security.who: Any caller the router reaches, carrying a principal with scopes and a tenant.
security.risk: The check composes scope, tenant and lifecycle state and raises about thirty lines below its own header. Anchoring it at the header is trap A1: the header cannot act, so a header anchor claims enforcement at a line that never enforces.

security.who: Any caller the router reaches; the only gate is the tenant comparison.
security.risk: Tenant-only. No scope is required to read, so any authenticated principal of a tenant sees every ticket in it.

tests_note: The suite was NOT run to build this table — the fixture ships no test suite of its own, by design: what exercises this tree is the coyomap regression suite in tests/, not tests inside the fixture. Every row below is inferred from that outside suite, and the gaps are the deliverable.

tests.label: Authorisation gate — the composed write predicate
tests.gap: Nothing exercises the scope/tenant/state composition. Its value to the regression suite is as an ANCHOR trap, not as behaviour under test.

tests.label: Ticket repository — the upsert that makes it the system of record

tests.why: feeds the repository's write anchor and the entity's definition line into anchor-drift as an 'is stored in' claim (trap A3)

tests.gap: The repository's own behaviour is never run; only the map's claims about it are checked.

tests.label: Publisher and consumer — channel naming and the drain loop
tests.gap: No test drives a message end to end. The messaging traps are asserted against the map and the tree, not against a running broker.

tests.label: The transition use case end to end
tests.gap: No integration test walks route to store to channel.

grounding.note: Every backbone edge in this map was authored directly against the fixture's own source, which is 1.5 kLOC of hand-written code the author of the map also wrote. That makes the grounding complete but NOT independent — there was no fresh-context skeptic pass, and this map has not been through Phase 4. Treat the number as a statement about coverage, not about adversarial confidence.

extras.heading: Coverage exceptions
extras.body:
- src/generated/: machine-emitted wire types regenerated from a schema; ~900 LOC folded into one component on purpose (trap G3). Reading it line by line buys nothing a reader needs.
- src/flatpack/: split into two cohesive components rather than one box (trap G2), so its individual files are deliberately not one-component-each.

extras.heading: Happy Path coverage
extras.body: - UC5: taking an advisory lock is an operator action before a bulk job, not part of the product story the spine tells. It keeps its own flow and stays off the walk.

extras.heading: Balance exceptions
extras.body:
- granularity: 28 components against a code-derived expectation of ~23 (band 13-33) — inside the band, recorded here only because the FILE cap binds on web/src/components (median file 24 LOC), which is trap G1 and would otherwise read as an unexplained agreement.
- entity-flows: not recorded — the flows DO touch entities, deliberately, so this token stays absent as the control.

extras.heading: Entry-point coverage
extras.body:
- http-route: complete — walked the six router.add registrations in build_router (src/entrypoints/http.py:34).
- event-consumer: complete — the fixture has exactly one consumer, CommentConsumer.run_forever.
- job: complete — the fixture has exactly one scheduled worker, ReportWorker on the SCHEDULE constant.
